title: "Low-Pass Switched Capacitor Filter Design"
subtitle: "Course Project · ECE 626 · Analog CMOS Circuit Design"
description: "Designed a 5th-order elliptic low-pass switched-capacitor filter meeting strict gain, ripple, and area constraints."
priority: 3
image: thumbnail.png
categories: [analog CMOS, switched-capacitor, filters]
abstract: "Students were tasked with designing a low-pass (LP) switched capacitor (SC) filter for a 12 MHz sampling frequency. The filter was required to have a passband from 0 - 0.9 MHz and a stopband from 1.8 - 6 MHz. The filter was required to have a gain of 0 dB in the passband and a gain of -50 dB in the stopband. The minimum capacitor size was required to be 0.05 pF. The filter was designed using MATLAB Signal Processing Toolbox and the Elliptic filter topology was selected as the best topology for the filter design. The poles and zeros of the filter were determined and the filter was designed to meet the specifications. The filter was implemented in Cadence Virtuoso. Dynamic range scaling and minimum capacitor scaling were performed to ensure the filter met the specifications and minimized chip area. The complete filter was simulated using macromodels representing the finite gain and bandwidth (BW) of the op-amps. Finally, the effects of charge injection, op-amp offset voltage, slew rate, bandwidth and finite gain were analyzed to determine the effects on the filter response."
bibliography: references.bib

: Filter Design Specifications. {#tbl-specs}

In order to ensure specifications were met, the designer chose to reduce the ripple to 0.1 dB in the passband and the stopband gain to -52 dB.

@tbl-orders computes the minimum order of each classic approximation for those targets; it reproduces the report's MATLAB results (Butterworth 11, Chebyshev I and II 7, elliptic 5).

```{ojs}
//| label: tbl-orders
//| tbl-cap: "Minimum order for each approximation, computed from the pre-warped band edges (0.1 dB ripple, 52 dB attenuation)."
Inputs.table(
  lowpassOrders(0.9e6, 1.8e6, 12e6, 0.1, 52).map(r => ({Approximation: r.name, "Exact bound": r.exact.toFixed(2), "Order": r.order})),
  {sort: null, layout: "auto"}
)
```

## Transfer function

The transfer function was then decomposed into the following second-order sections:

$$
H_1(z) = \frac{0.005133z^2 + 0.005133z}{z^2 - 0.744z}
$$ {#eq-h1}

$$
H_2(z) = \frac{z^2 - 1.357z + 1}{z^2 - 1.652z + 0.8898}
$$ {#eq-h2}

$$
H_3(z) = \frac{z^2 - 0.7563z + 1}{z^2 - 1.537z + 0.6723}
$$ {#eq-h3}

The 5th order elliptic filter was designed by cascading a standard active SC linear filter with two Tow-Thomas Biquads. The Tow-Thomas Biquad is a popular choice for SC filters due to its simplicity and ease of design. By simply matching the coefficients of the transfer functions derived in MATLAB to the symbolic transfer function derived by analyzing the circuit, one can easily obtain the SC realization of the filter. All three stages were derived from examples found in [@carusone2012].

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
fs = 12e6
// Cascade of (1)-(3); H1's common factor of z cancels, leaving a 5th-order H(z).
num = polyMul(polyMul([0.005133, 0.005133], [1, -1.357, 1]), [1, -0.7563, 1])
den = polyMul(polyMul([1, -0.744], [1, -1.652, 0.8898]), [1, -1.537, 0.6723])
```

```{ojs}
//| label: fig-pz
//| fig-cap: "Poles (×) and zeros (○) of the cascade, found numerically from the coefficients in (1)–(3). All zeros lie on the unit circle; all poles lie inside it."
{
  const z = roots(num), p = roots(den);
  const circle = linspace(0, 2 * Math.PI, 361).map(t => ({x: Math.cos(t), y: Math.sin(t)}));
  return Plot.plot({ariaLabel: "Pole-zero plot in the z-plane with the unit circle dashed. Five zeros lie on the unit circle: conjugate pairs at angles corresponding to 1.576 MHz and 2.259 MHz, and one at z = −1 (6 MHz). Five poles lie inside it: one real pole at z = 0.744 and conjugate pairs at radius 0.820 and 0.943.",
    width: 460, height: 420, style: plotStyle, grid: true,
    x: {domain: [-1.5, 1.5], label: "Real part"}, y: {domain: [-1.25, 1.25], label: "Imaginary part"},
    marks: [
      Plot.ruleX([0], {stroke: palette.grid}), Plot.ruleY([0], {stroke: palette.grid}),
      Plot.line(circle, {x: "x", y: "y", stroke: palette.muted, strokeDasharray: "3,3"}),
      Plot.dot(z, {x: "re", y: "im", r: 6, stroke: palette.accent, strokeWidth: 2, fill: "none"}),
      Plot.dot(p, {x: "re", y: "im", r: 6, symbol: "times", stroke: palette.high, strokeWidth: 2})
    ]
  });
}
```

```{ojs}
//| label: fig-mag
//| fig-cap: "Magnitude response of the cascade from 0 to 6 MHz (fs = 12 MHz), evaluated on the unit circle from (1)–(3). Shaded regions are excluded by the specification: below −0.25 dB in the passband, above −50 dB in the stopband."
{
  const pts = linspace(1, 6e6, 1500).map(f => freqz(num, den, f, fs)).map(d => ({f: d.f / 1e6, dB: Math.max(d.dB, -100)}));
  return Plot.plot({ariaLabel: "Magnitude response from 0 to 6 MHz. The gain stays between −0.03 and −0.13 dB up to 0.9 MHz, falls steeply with notches near 1.58 and 2.26 MHz, and stays at or below −52 dB from 1.8 to 6 MHz, clear of both shaded specification regions.",
    width: 640, height: 320, style: plotStyle, grid: true,
    x: {label: "Frequency (MHz)", domain: [0, 6]}, y: {label: "Magnitude (dB)", domain: [-100, 5]},
    marks: [
      Plot.rect([{x1: 1.8, x2: 6, y1: -50, y2: 5}], {x1: "x1", x2: "x2", y1: "y1", y2: "y2", fill: palette.shade, fillOpacity: 0.6}),
      Plot.rect([{x1: 0, x2: 0.9, y1: -100, y2: -0.25}], {x1: "x1", x2: "x2", y1: "y1", y2: "y2", fill: palette.shade, fillOpacity: 0.6}),
      Plot.line(pts, {x: "f", y: "dB", stroke: palette.accent, strokeWidth: 1.6}),
      Plot.text([{x: 3.9, y: -42, t: "stopband limit −50 dB"}], {x: "x", y: "y", text: "t", fill: palette.muted})
    ]
  });
}
```

```{ojs}
//| label: fig-passband
//| fig-cap: "Passband detail, 0–0.9 MHz. Computed from the published coefficients; the reported Cadence simulation shows ripple under 0.16 dB."
{
  const pts = linspace(1, 0.9e6, 600).map(f => freqz(num, den, f, fs)).map(d => ({f: d.f / 1e6, dB: d.dB}));
  return Plot.plot({ariaLabel: "Passband magnitude from 0 to 0.9 MHz on a −0.3 to 0.05 dB scale. The response stays between −0.03 and −0.13 dB, above the dashed −0.25 dB ripple limit.",
    width: 640, height: 260, style: plotStyle, grid: true,
    x: {label: "Frequency (MHz)"}, y: {label: "Magnitude (dB)", domain: [-0.3, 0.05]},
    marks: [
      Plot.ruleY([-0.25], {stroke: palette.high, strokeDasharray: "4,3"}),
      Plot.text([{x: 0.05, y: -0.235, t: "ripple limit −0.25 dB"}], {x: "x", y: "y", text: "t", textAnchor: "start", fill: palette.high}),
      Plot.line(pts, {x: "f", y: "dB", stroke: palette.accent, strokeWidth: 1.6})
    ]
  });
}
```

```{ojs}
//| label: fig-step
//| fig-cap: "Step response of the cascade at fs = 12 MHz, from the difference equation of (1)–(3)."
{
  const y = stepResponse(num, den, 72).map((v, n) => ({t: n / fs * 1e6, v}));
  return Plot.plot({ariaLabel: "Step response sampled at 12 MHz over about 6 µs. The output rises from 0, overshoots to a peak of 1.17 at about 1.08 µs, and settles at 0.99, staying within 2% after about 3.3 µs.",
    width: 640, height: 260, style: plotStyle, grid: true,
    x: {label: "Time (µs)"}, y: {label: "Amplitude", domain: [0, 1.25]},
    marks: [
      Plot.ruleY([1], {stroke: palette.grid}),
      Plot.line(y, {x: "t", y: "v", stroke: palette.accent, strokeWidth: 1.4, curve: "step-after"}),
      Plot.dot(y, {x: "t", y: "v", r: 1.8, fill: palette.accent})
    ]
  });
}
```

## Conclusion

In conclusion, the designer was able to design a 5th order elliptic low-pass switched capacitor filter that met the specifications provided. The filter was designed using MATLAB Signal Processing Toolbox and implemented using macromodels for the op-amps and switches in Cadence Virtuoso. The poles and zeros of the filter were determined and the filter was designed to meet the specifications. Dynamic range scaling and minimum capacitor scaling were performed to ensure the filter met the specifications and minimized chip area. The effects of charge injection, op-amp offset voltage, slew rate, bandwidth and finite gain were analyzed to determine the effects on the filter response.
